p: Pardon?
Yes, we’re– today, we’re exceeding the limit, but for the most part over the period of year since we started with the lowest limit that we are at today, we’ve met the standard, yes.

Okay, alright. I just– sometimes it’s good to check in on issues every 20 years and see if– like, how that’s going. And thank you for that. I’m sure that the Long Island Sound and– both the Sound and Jamaica Bay will, you know, benefit from that. And great, thank you. I appreciate that. Let me get to some of my prepared– oh, let me– so that was 730A. And the light pollution, not going to do that now. And on drinking fountains, we had very comprehensive testimony on

that. Let me go to the– going to pause for one second here. Here’s what we’re going to do, I’m going to try to be conservative with my time. I’m having counsel go through the questions that– make sure we hit the ones that we really need to get the administration on the record for. In the meantime, being the nice guy that I am, I’m going to open up the questioning to my colleagues on the committee who have important concerns, other places to be, and to go– and we have two Council Members who are signed up to ask questions. I’m going to recognize Council Member Wong for questions. So, Council Member Wong, the floor is yours.

Okay, thank you, Chair. My question pertains to the edits and issues the administration has for the light bill, that’s Intro 804. I think one of the crucial things that is lost in the discussions, my office has been having with the administration is just how simple this bill is. We are tackling a simple problem, offensively bright outdoor lights in residential neighborhoods. The solution is simple, make them illegal without a proper covering. That’s all. I appreciate the technical concerns. They have been very helpful in

getting the best version of this bill, but I worry the administration is overcomplicating this scenario. Before I get to my questions, there are Department of Buildings inspectors that go around my district and write tickets if you forget to turn on the light outside of your house, you get a big ticket. Right? And then the fines get higher. So, there are agencies out there enforcing the law that if you don’t turn on your lights at night, you will get fined. So, I can tell you that because I have received these tickets before. So, I want to address a few of the concerns. There was a issue about lux versus lumens, and I want to defer to the experts on this. If you think lux is a better unit of measurement, then I’m open to changing it to lux or perhaps your light meters detects lux and not lumens. You know, I’m open to change that. And there was an issue about more time to prepare for enforcement, and if the administration thinks it needs more time for the enforcement, I’m ready to give you more time. And regarding the penalty, if the proposed $50 is not steep enough to reduce offenders, I’m ready to increase the fine. And finally, how is this enforcement done? Now, I do not want members of any

Department driving around the city looking for offenders. If a neighbor has an issue, just like with any other non-emergency problem in the city and they will call 311, and then will start the process of getting solutions. So, I hope to continue to have conversations with the administration so we can clear up any confusion of this bill and introduce a simple solution to a simple problem. Thank you.
And also, before the witness begins to speak to the Council Member’s question, you know, just in case the time elapses, you know, please continue with your answer.
Was there a specific question about–

[interposing] Oh, yeah, I’m going to. That’s my feedback after looking at the edits that was made by the administration, but I’m going to go ahead. Currently, I know the Department of Buildings, but I don’t know if DEP or any other agency– are there any other agencies accept complaints about excessively bright residential lights?

My understanding is that they do not. I think if there

are more specific questions about what DOB enforces, that we might be able to answer those. Yeah. We can have DOB come up and answer this specifically.
Okay, sure, sure, please.
DEP doesn’t do any like enforcement at all?
Okay.

Could you raise your right hand, please? Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions? Thank you. If you could just state your name and title for the record.
And also, feel free to give your full answer, notwithstanding the buzzer going off in a minute.
Thank you. My name’s Renaldo Hilton [sp?]. I’m the Assistant Commissioner for Enforcement Inspections at Department of Buildings.

So, my question is DOB or any of your divisions currently accept

complaints about excessively bright residential lights?
No, sir.
So, no–
[interposing] Not that I’m aware.
So you’re aware of no city agencies by taking these complaints?
I’m not aware if DOB’s accepting any complaints.
Okay. So want to ask the panel, which agency is best suited to enforce this bill?

I think that those are some of the things that we’re talking about council. I don’t think we want to debate which agency is responsible or would most likely to be responsible or would be most likely to be responsible. I think it might depend on some of the specifics that are agreed upon in red lining process.
Okay. A question about cost to detect excessive lighting, you’d like light meters. How much do you estimate from–
[interposing] We don’t know–
We’re being on a limit, I’ll give you a little–
Last question.
I will give you the I’ll– give you the latitutde to ask this question, Chair.
Thank you, thank you. Okay. okay. How much do you estimate it will cost to purchase and maintain equipment needed to enforcement this bill, like such as light meters.

So, Council Member, we are not equipped right now to give an estimate, because we don’t really have– since this is kind of new to us, you know, to do that we would have to– there would be some kind of agreement on what type of meters would be appropriate and all that and then some research on those costs. We were not able right not to give an estimate on cost.
Okay. There’s a follow-up. How much time do you need– would you need to purchase the appropriate equipment and begin enforcing the bill?
I’m not prepared to give an answer to that right now.
Alright. So, hopefully you can give me an estimate that–
Sure, we can get back to you.
Alright, I’ll save my other questions for round two. Thank you, Chair.

Sure. I’ll say in my neighborhood of Jamaica Estates. There’s a lot of people that have like obnoxious lights that are, you know, shining into other people’s homes I know that– accessibility we ge complaints about it. I mean, you know, and the civic that I used to be Chair of, President of or whatever, and get some– I should ask my case workers what they do when these get these complaints because we get complaints about it. I mean, in my community it’s almost like a competition as to who can have more obnoxious light. You know, it’s like– sorry, you know. But it just– sometimes it just gets a little bit much. I just– shouldn't indulge people to speak from the audience. But I’m just saying that I recognize your problem, and you

know, look forard–, and you know look forward to working with that.
Thank you, Chair.
Okay, yes. I’m happy to recognize Council Member Epstein for questions.

Yeah, can I– just on the water quality testing, 730A, I appreciate that it’s a shared priority. So, I’m wondering where you think the issues are in trying to ensure we have higher quality water and kind of the issues you think are flagged right now, because we hear a lot of concerns around quality of water, quality of waterways. You know, what is the best approach to ensuring that the public feels like we have that high quality water?

The Harbor’s got some of the cleanest water we’ve ever seen it have, not even recent years, in decades and decades. We’ve got two main monitoring programs that hit about 158 sites all around 48 different waterways. I guess some of the questions that we’d like to work out with Council is, what the primary objective is. Is this a health objective? In which

case it might help us tailor the types of tests that are most relevant, probably more towards fecal and bacteria versus algae.
Right.
And then–
[interposing] Or heavy metals, too, or concerns around heavy metals.
Yeah, and then which the turnaround on the tests, you know, can vary. So how quickly you want to get the information versus the type of test you have.
Right.
How the information is made available. What’s going to be the most useful way, putting, you know, data into the universe where no one can access it isn’t probably what you have in mind.
Right.

So, I think that those are some of the issues that we’d like to work through. We’d like to work through how long it takes us to get and to increase a program like this, resources certainly. The way that we do testing right now, the same people that drive the boats that do

testing for us are also driving boats to move our sludge and wastewater treatment around. This bill doesn’t offer, as written right now, any flexibility for emergencies, two core operations for this agency. So, I think those are some of the challenges that we want to work through. I think there are definitely ways to do that and to work through this so that we can have more instantaneous information about the testing. And some of it is just having more information about the testing that we already do in a way that the public can understand and access it.

Right. Thank you. Can I turn our attention to the water drinking fountains? I mean, I– so, there are drinking fountains in my district that have never been operational. They’re there. The infrastructure’s there. They’re just never open. You go to Astor [sp?] Place, there’s a water fountain right by the subway station. It’s just not operational. So, but it’s there. DOT’s like we don’t know, and DEP’s like we don’t know. And who– like it’s Parks, like– like, we want to create amenities. We all agree on that goal, so how do we ensure that something like that’s in Tompkins [sp?] Square Park or at Astor Place

become a functional water fountain for New Yorkers to have access to?

Thank you, Council Member. The water fountains that are in Parks are our responsibility. I’m not familiar with the one you mentioned at Astor Place. You mentioned it’s by a subway station. That’s probably not park land, so that would not be ours.
It’s funny, because the BID [sic] says it’s not ours. DOT says it’s not theirs.

Well, it may have been built years ago by somebody, but it’s not– if it’s not on park land, it’s not our jurisdiction. We don’t have the authority. It’s simply– I don’t know any other way to say it, but if it’s not on park land, it’s not the responsibility of Parks, and again, we have over 3,400 drinking fountains. We’re by far the largest provider. We have the majority of the burden and the honor of delivering–
[interposing] Right.
clean drinking water to citizens and visitors in New York. We take that very seriously. So, we expend our resources on maintaining what is ours.

Okay. The one in Tompkins Square Park has been maintained in 30 years. I’ve lived by Tompkins Square Park for over 30 years. That water fountain that leaks today has leaked for over 30 yeawrs. We talked to Parks Department about it. How do we get like a new– like, how do we get prioritized that water fountain in Tompkins Square Park to be upgraded so it’s usable?
Well, I believe I’m familiar with the one you’re mentionoing, and you mentioned it leaks. It does. You and I have both looked at it together.
Yes.
It works. It leaks.
I mean, it works like it spurts right into the air, yeah.

But it– folks can get drinking water out of it. It’s also leaking out of the bottom. We will look at it again.

We do not replace individual drinking fountains as per an operational. All of the replacement of drinking fountains is done through a capital process. So, the capital reconstruction–
[interposing] So, if I give you capital money, you’ll replace it?
We would love to talk to you about that.

Okay. And this– so I go to DOT and they’re saying it’s not us, that’s not our water fountain. We don’t know. We know it’s there. And we go to the BID, and they’re like, we didn’t put it in. We don’t know where it goes. And we go to you and you say we– it’s not us. So, but we’re all the city, right? Can’t someone tell us why there’s a water fountain in place with a– and why it doesn’t work? Like someone’s got to have the answer, right? Who is it?

I got an answer, I think. It might have been put in the pre-DEP days of the old City Department of Public Works, and in that case, in my book, I think it should fall to DEP, because they’re the successor agency to the old New York City Department of Public Works.
So, can DEP look at this?

We’re happy to go out and see if we can answer this riddle for who might have ownership of this one particular fountain. We’d like to stress that DEP doesn’t operate any fountains at all. We don’t have any program to maintain them. So, a working water fountain is great. Nobody wants to drink from a dirty, non-maintained water fountain.
Then we get the BID to maintain it. They’re the BID there. They can maintain it.
Yeah, but you got to fix it.
Yeah, we got to fix it.
Right.

The installation of 10 water fountains, we’re talking about hundreds of thousands of dollars which we would get from where, and what part of DEP would you like us to not replace the water main on your block?

That’s where like– those are some of the things that we’re trying to– right?
How about just do this, can you find out who’s in charge?
Yeah.
We’ll find out who owns it and then whether or not it’s operational and we can make it operational.
Thank you.

I just think, and not that my opinion means anything, but you know, barring any other agency stepping forward, you know, I think DEP is like the default agency for the conveyance of– you know, of water infrastructure. I just– I think, you know, like– you know, when everyone else sits down, you know, and then like the music stops. I think DEP is the agency that’s still standing up, you know? To put it that way. That’s what I think. You’re the councilman. You tell them whatever you want, you know? They should be afraid of you, you know? If you give them money, like they’ll do it, you know? Okay. Beth, you talked– and you mentioned a little bit about the– about the testing that both, you know, DEP does and the

Department of Health does. Can you speak with a little more specificity in describing the testing that you do, DEP does, in the Harbor Survey? Just a little more specificity as to what happens in that.

Sure, sure. Thank you, Councilman. The Harbor Survey Program, we test weekly from May to October and then monthly from November to April which largely monitors what DOH does at beaches when people are most likely to use it. The program tests primarily five different parameters related to water quality, dissolved oxygen bacteria, so fecal coliform, chlorophyl A, water clarity, and nitrogen.
Okay. Now–
[interposing] Those are 84 sites that that program targets specifically.

Now, do they tend to be like near shore sites like the Department of Health probably does, or are they kind of like in the middle of the water body, like, you know, out a ways or whatever? Depending upon like the watercraft that you use to go out and do that, is it near shore or do you get a better read, or the read that you’re asked

to get– or do you take those out aways and get those readings in like the middle of the water body as opposed to the near shore environment?

It’s both. No, it makes sense. I was actually looking for and asking about a map so that I could answer that same question myself earlier this morning. Yeah, it’s both. So we do take from the middle of some water bodies, but primarily overall it’s right near your shorelines.
Okay.
And your outfalls, especially.

Great. Thank you. Going down on the question set here. That one’s already been answered. Oh, okay. That’s the next one? Okay, this is a question directly from Counsel, Counsel to the Committee– so this comes from the top here. For DEP, it’s about 795, the water fountain bill. Regarding Intro 795, is DEP– oh, this is like– okay. Oh, if DEP is not the appropriate agency to install water fountains in non-parks public spaces, then which agency would be appropriate? We just kind of had this– we talked about this a little bit. So,

I guess I’m asking it again. So, you know, because– you know, people watching online and whatever, and we’re talking to the agencies that are most involved in this kind of infrastructure, and the– you know, and the answer of, you know, I don’t know is– I’m not sure that’s giving a lot of confidence to people who may be watching this hearing. Like, somebody knows, you know?
Chairman, that’s a fair point. I don’t think it’s about–
[interposing] This is an opportunity for you to clean it. Just clean it.
Thank you for the opportunity.
Plant the flag. Just do it.

However, the thing that we have to think about when making these decisions– listen, it’s whatever agency, you know, the administration or council decides that it should be. I think some of our hesitation on this is that we don’t have this infrastructure in place now. The way that we pay for upgrades to the system, fixing your

sewer, your water mains, is your water bill. So, as we think about doing these things, one thing we’re also trying to do is keep your water bill low, so that, you know, especially–
[interposing] [inaudible] concerned about that–
in times like these.

with the rental payment. He could care less about how far rates go up. He’s going to take $300-something million out of water and sewer money and give it to who knows. Just a, you know, general, you know, city operations. Great agencies, Fire Department, Police Department, Parks Defendants, you know, the Department of Records and Information Services, like who knows? He’s going to put this wherever it is. He’s going to– you know, he’s taking water and sewer money and just going to spread it away, just put it anywhere. Just like a– I couldn't resist the temptation that, you know, while DEP is very concerned about water rates, we have a Mayor that is not concerned about water rates. We’ll have to see this year if when he does a rental payment, if he charges and water and sewer customers

in real time for the rental payment or whether he takes it out of reserves which he’s– you know, he hasn’t done anything yet. But that’s what Adams did. He took it out of– largely out of Water Finance Authority Reserves. I don’t think the people who, you know, rate the bonds, you know, really appreciate hundreds and millions of dollars leaving the system and not being paid for, but being taken out of reserves. people, you know, like the bond holders, you know, Wall Street types don’t like to see reserves, you know, depleted. If you’re going to charge rental payment, then stand up and charge it. So you’re going to charge $300-something million in water and sewer, $40 million a rate point, you know, divide that into $300 million. Just raise points and just raise the water rates eight or nine points just to cover the rental payment, and explain that to the people that we took– that we raise your water rates nine percent, you know, just to cover the rental payment that doesn’t go to water and sewer at all, and then we're going to raise it on top of that, you know, to keep up with the growing demands of the system. Like, going from 1.75 inches, you know, storm sewer capacity to 2.1 to all the other things

that the agency does. So, you know, the Mayor’s picking your pocket, but you’re not going to say that. And so I digress, but you– you [inaudible] give me wonderful answer.

One of the things that we’re thinking about and would like to, you know, work with Council on and maybe do a pilot on is a public/private partnership. How do we put water fountains in places that are very accessible to people? We’re very proud of our water. You know, it didn’t get its nickname of Champagne of Water for no reason.
Right.
So, we want to make that as accessible as possible. There might be some more creative ways to do that. I think that’s the thing–
[interposing] This is going to be the test case right here. This is going to be the test case.

So, that’s one of the things that we’re looking at specifically, but we do– we don’t have the infrastructure in place right now, and so if you’re asking what some of the

challenges are, I think that we would put that at the top.

Okay. Well, Harvey, this should be a thing, because we’ve got these– we got these orphan– you know, we have these orphan water fountains like all over the place, and like, what is– yours is going to be the poster fountain for all this. And so, I want to get invited to the ribbon cutting once we find out–
[inaudible]

Hey, you know, next four– I’m going to be 69 years old in a couple of weeks, so you know. These, like, four-year time horizons is starting to scare me a little bit, you know? So, now the– yeah. I’m serving out my term. This is– yeah, I’m serving out my term. That’s a lock. Plus my wife would be mad. And so, okay. So, we did that. We did that. He wants to go in on second round. So– you going to come for second round? Okay, so I had a think about the light, but you know, we don’t want to– I don’t want to light up the hearing with too many light questions. You could have giggled at that. I got nothing. I got nothing. I got nothing. You know, I’m trying to work with a

tough crowd here. Whatever. Now, my comments may not be funny, but Sham Tarricks [sp?] socks are funny, and so I appreciate that. I like the socks. I wear funny socks, too. I recognize Council Member Wong.

Thank you, Chair. Well, I just want to point out that in my district whenever we have a sidewalk that’s cracking or a facade that’s any kind of violations, the Department of Buildings will be there like within a couple a days and issue citations and summonses. We have residents that regularly get trees that with roots that uplifted the concrete, and they get hefty summonses or they have to replace the sidewalk or else. You know, there will be even subject to even heftier fines. So, I know the enforcement is out there. The inspectors are out there at night looking at sidewalks, looking at trees, and I’m sure that they could also look at the lights, and if it’s too bright or if it’s not in compliance they can issue a warning before they issue summonses. I know the enforcement teams are out there, and it’s a matter of one extra item they’re going to look into it, and because light pollution is a serious issue in my

district for residences, and I’m going to ask the administration to look into the matter, whether it’s Department of Buildings to add an extra item to enforcement or even DEP when you look at the water, when you look at– when you look at the other issues in the streets. That is my suggestion to you.

I’ll certainly let some of the other agencies speak about that. I think that we would have concerns about taking away from what our crews are doing at night to make sure– to cover the entire city and make sure our water infrastructure is working. I think that it’s– it sounds like a very easy answer that’s very complex. That would prob– the people that we have working overnight to detect leaks and fix water mains and sewers are not trained in light detection. They’ve got– usually they’re emergency– like, they’re working on emergencies overnight. So, I think that that’s– we would have concerns about distracting with that additional responsibility. Sure, there might be another creative way to come up with doing this besides using engineers and emergency contractors, some of the people that we have on overnight to help us detect leaks from a DEP’s perspective. Certainly,

Parks, DOB, I’ll let them speak to that, but I think that would be our perspective.
Does DEP have inspectors? Do you inspect private residential properties?
No. We don’t inspect private re– no. No private residence. We don’t touch private properties, only the water mains and sewers in the middle of the street.
Okay. So, that’s perhaps something that the Department of Buildings will look into, can you answer that?
So, Council Member,–
[interposing] Yes.

the Department of Buildings do have inspectors operating at night. However, those inspectors are responding to emergencies. This is a night crew usually to fires, to different things that happen afterhours, and we certainly do not, as I said before, have the capability of, you know, measuring light. We don’t have– even the inspectors are not trained on those things. So, there would be some challenges into

getting up to speed to be able to do that. Could we do that? Of course, but it would be– it would be intensive resources that would be needed to implement something like that, and we’d have to see how this bill works out in–

[interposing] We’ll talk about funding if this needs– this bill needs to be backed with certain amount of funding. We’d be glad to talk about that. Question, is lumens or lux, which one is a more appropriate measure of light, since this was heavily edited? So, I want to hear from you. Can anybody answer that?
I could not personally, but I believe they settled on lumens.
Lumens?
Is it lux? Lux, I’m sorry.
Lux.
I don’t know the difference myself.
Thank you. Okay, my final question. How bright do outdoor residential lights need to be safety reasons? How bright?
So, that would have to be, you know, settled into the legislation, right? We’d have to– again, this is not something the Department of Buildings does right now on a regular basis.

That’s why we have a problem with these bright lights. People due to various reasons buy the biggest, brightest lamp fixture, put them in the back yards, front yards, and then we have this problem today.
I understand.

And the Chair agrees. Thank you. And I want to– my final question. Color temperatures, are there any color temperatures that are known to be more or less associated with the negative impacts of light pollution?
Right. So, I just– from my experts– I don’t think we have that expertise right now in our department to actually come up with an answer to.

Okay. So, I think, Chair, we can conclude that this is an issue that

there’s no– no agency is responsible for enforcing or for addressing, and we–
[interposing] Yeah, we got a lot of like orphan topics. We got orphan drinking wells. We got orphan issues and stuff. Like, who’s got the ball on this? And so–
[interposing] I did not hear anyone stepping forward.
Yeah, it is what it is. These are all well-intentioned people–
[interposing] Okay.

trying their best to, you know, give us the answers that we seek, but you know, you’ve uncovered an area that heretofore has, you know, hasn’t really required a lot of oversight or whatever. And people put lights on their porch, and you know, DOT makes decisions about how bright the street lights are. Recently they went from like moderately bright to very bright. Okay. You know? And so somebody put some brain power into that. So, but we’ve uncovered an area where there is, you know, not a lot being done on it now, other that what DOT does to regulate the street lights.

This is a whole area that the city needs to take a look at, and you’re the pioneer. So,--
[interposing] Well–
[interposing] And Harvey’s with these other fixtures, the drinking water fixtures that are– you know, they are sort of unclaimed by any city agency. This is why we’re here, Phil. We try to–

[interposing] I hope we can work with the administration to come up with the best solution to this with appropriate funding, because it’s clearly a problem in residential homes, and it’s definitely distracting– is a distraction to the neighbors and the residents living near these homes with bright outdoor lights.
